work.title: Life of Rabbula
work.edition: Machine translation (claude-opus-5-5, Patristica, 2026-10-30) of: Julian Joseph Overbeck S. Ephraemi Syri, Rabulae episcopi Edesseni, Balaei aliorumque Oper; TEI by J. E. Walters, Digital Syriac Corpus (syriaccorpus.org 490)

paragraphs.text: The triumphs of Mar Rabbula, bishop of the blessed city of Edessa.

My brothers, moved by zeal for the love of Christ, we are drawing for you in writing, beloved, a portrait of the excellent way of life of Mar Rabbula the bishop, the glory of our city. May he be for us and for every generation an inspiring goal, so that we may be nourished by his virtues. In the arena of righteousness he proved valiant, and in hard battles with the rulers he was victorious. By his wisdom he overcame the cunning of the Slanderer. He openly despised the world and its desires. He trampled the enemy's power through his warfare. He subdued the body and its passions by his endurance. He overcame Satan, his enemy, through his struggle, and he turned back to the truth those whom Satan had led astray. The cunning [?] of the sweet [?] of sin he subdued by the keenness of his endurance. He helped people by his words, and his deeds benefited many. He gladdened the angels, and they marveled at his purity. He praised his Lord and magnified him by his faith. He found his soul

and won [?] his life, and the Spirit of God rested on him all his life long, until he carried off the crown of uprightness from every contest of asceticism, adorned with a good end worthy of God. It is right for us, then, to set down a full record of the divine conduct of this renowned victor, so that it may be for us and for every generation an image of his triumphs, an inspiring goal by which people may be nourished, as they are by the excellent fathers of renowned name, whose excellences are set up as portraits in times both ancient and new, and given body in the colours of the writings of the holy books.

Now this blessed Rabbula was a pagan from his youth, because his father too was a pagan, and a priest. It was by his hands that the wicked Julian sacrificed to the demons when he went down to the war against the Persians. His mother, however, was a believer. She struggled with her husband, that he might turn to the fear of Christ, and she kept at it continually; but she could not overcome the strength of his tyrannical will so as to turn him to the truth. He in turn pressed the believing woman in every way, but he could not bring the strength of her freedom in Jesus into bondage to sin. So each of them held to their own. From them was born one who triumphed in everything, Rabbula the zealous, a second Josiah, if such a comparison does justice to the holy man's honour. His mother entrusted her child to a believing nurse. When he grew up he was trained in the learning of the Greeks, as the son of the great rich men of their city, Qenneshrin. And early on his mother took for him

a believing wife. His wife and his mother kept urging him to turn from his father's paganism to faith in Christ, but he would not be persuaded by them. He prided himself on the famous position of authority and honour that the emperor had allotted him. Then a good occasion arose: he went to inspect his villages in the region of the desert of Qenneshrin. Within the bounds of one of his lands there was a solitary monastery belonging to the blessed Abraham the recluse. His servants and the inhabitants of that place told him that foreign brothers lived in this monastery, and that astonishing powers of healing were worked by their hands through Christ, the God of the Christians. When he heard this, the good report of the signs amazed him, and the news of the monk's triumphs fell on his soul like an ocean. As the fire of love for this adored name of Jesus ran through his heart, his mind began to be divided over his paganism. Swiftly and urgently, under God's guidance, it brought him to see this blessed man, so that he might see with his own eyes the power of the wonders of Jesus, whom he hated. It was like Paul, who at first persecuted Jesus, until the blaze of the heavenly voice, when he bowed [?] beneath the yoke of the cross, snatched him away from Judaism to the truth, just as it snatched Rabbula from paganism to Christianity. And because signs are needed by those who do not believe, that good Lord who cares for his servants went ahead of him to gather him into life, as he did with the Samaritan woman

and with Nathanael, through the small sign by which each was caught for life. A woman was brought to the victorious Abraham whose flesh had been wasting from an illness of long duration, and whose limbs were paralysed. When the blessed Rabbula saw this wonder, he went away marveling within himself at what had happened, and by the power of Christ he began to be divided over his paganism. He said to himself in his heart, as he later told us himself: "If it seems a mockery to you to deny their gods in the temples of the pagans and to confess the crucified God, see what the memory of his cross has done to your soul through the healing of that woman, and settle the matter for yourself." When his mother saw that his colour had changed, and heard from those who had been with him about the divine visitation that had come before his eyes, she hurried in her joy to the blessed Eusebius, bishop of her city, and told him what had happened to her son. Eusebius sent for him and expounded many things to him about Christ from the Scriptures. Then he reflected that help from others would support his own words. So he quickly arose, took him, and brought him to the illustrious Acacius, bishop of the city of Aleppo. For they were brothers in Christ and had been trained together in the honourable life of a monastery. When Acacius heard the reason for their coming, he was overjoyed, and his compassion went out to Rabbula. He began to say to him: "My son, you cannot grasp the power of the truth, that it is the truth, unless you know that this thing

which you know is error." Rabbula answered him: "How can I know that what I know is error, unless that very truth, by its light, shows me truth and error distinctly?" Acacius took up this reply skilfully and said to him: "You can know the truth if you know that you do not yet know it." Rabbula said: "Knowing that I do not know the truth would not be knowledge of the truth. It would only be a conviction about my error, that it is error. But I want to know the truth itself." Acacius said to him: "Believe in our Lord Jesus, that he is the Son of God, and the truth is wise enough to lead you to itself." He said: "And by what means can I come to know Christ? For if he is the very truth, he is the one I am compelled to know." Eusebius said to him: "The truth itself will make itself known to you, if you strip yourself of your own knowledge and come to need knowledge of it." Rabbula said: "And how can I forget these things, when I remember them even against my will?" Eusebius said: "When the abiding remembrance of Jesus enters and dwells in your soul, it will drive away all the evils that struggle within you, and they will flee from you, as darkness rolls back before the rays of light." When they had talked at length among themselves about the faith, he vowed to go and pray at the shrine of the victorious martyrs Cosmas and Damian. They provided him with prayer and sent him off rejoicing. As he stood in the sanctuary he saw a man he knew

who had been blind, and now could see. He marveled at the power of the cross, and he was all the more astonished at the wonder God worked in him, in his own person: the Lord opened his lips, and he gave new praise to God, to the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. He gave alms there, stirred by what he had seen and heard, and went back on his way, despising himself for the error he had lived in until then. He came to Acacius and revealed to him how, as he stood praying, God had put praise in his mouth, and he confessed the faith of Jesus before him. When Acacius heard this, he rejoiced in his faith and said to him: "My son, when the fire of God's love runs through a person's heart, all the desires, together with all the thickets of sin, are stirred up in it and burn away, and he alone is purified in them sevenfold and made white." Then the bishops Acacius and Eusebius took him again to the monastery of the holy Marcianus the recluse, and to the blessed Abraham whom we mentioned above. With rich words they strengthened his mind and urged him to take up the monastic life. Rabbula agreed with them and said: "Since I have truly hoped in the Lord and believed in the Son of God, I have vowed my whole soul to God. I will forsake the world completely and cleave to God entirely, and I will be enclosed in a monastery as you are. But this is my desire: to go to Jerusalem and see the holy places, and to be baptized in the Jordan, where Christ himself was baptized as a pattern for us." When these fathers heard this, they rejoiced, provided him with prayer and sent him off. When he entered Jerusalem,

the blessed Mar Rabbula prayed before Golgotha with many tears and much anguish. He entered the tomb of our Lord and the cave in which he was born, and went up to the church of the Ascension. He gave alms to the poor and went down from there to the Jordan. At once he persuaded the priests, and he recited the faith before them, and they anointed him and baptized him. As soon as he came up out of the water, the linen garment wrapped around his body, as is the custom for the spiritual bridegrooms of Christ, was seen to be covered all over, gleaming on every side, with the one healing medicine of Christ's blood in the form of crosses. All who were there, when they saw this great wonder, looked and were amazed; they trembled and fear seized them. In haste they fell down and knelt in prayer before God, and with a loud voice praised God for all the mighty works they had seen. When he had shared in the holy mysteries of the body and blood of our Lord, and had been filled with the whole divine mystery, he returned to his city, rejoicing in his faith, firm in his hope, exulting in his love, filled with his affection, and receiving the grace of God.

As soon as the blessed Rabbula had been baptized and had gone back down to his city and entered his house, like a blessed man who has fulfilled his vow, and like the wise merchant who goes out in search of fine pearls, having found the pearl of his hope, he went and sold everything he had and bought it. He distributed his gold and silver and everything he owned to the needy, so that his almsgiving reached even the holy ones and the poor of Edessa, the city which, as he had prophesied, he was destined to receive as his own

inheritance. For the mystery of Christ had gone ahead and sold it to him, with his almsgiving as the pledge, through its poor [?], as also to the rest of the regions. For he understood clearly within himself that the desire of this world and the thought of riches, like thickets and thorns, choke the seed of God's word in a soul that is not careful, and it bears no fruit. For this reason he hurried to throw off the whole heavy burden of the bonds of wealth, so that the word of God he had received might grow abundantly in his hidden life and yield fruit thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold. So he received with joy our Lord's commandment: "Whoever does not leave all his possessions cannot be my disciple." Quickly he scattered and gave all he owned to the poor, so that his righteousness might endure forever. He also sold his villages and duly divided their price among the needy, so that through their hands his goods might be brought into the heavenly treasury, and his treasures be kept for him there to his profit. His servants, too, both those born in his house and those bought with his money, he set free, every one; he provided for each of them and sent them away in peace. Some of them he instructed [?], made disciples, and brought into monasteries. His blessed mother gladly gave up all she owned and took on the yoke of Christ, and his wife did the same. His sons, who were still young, he trained as disciples and placed in monasteries. So he stripped himself of everything he possessed, that he might gain the Lord of all possessions. When he had made himself solitary, according to our Lord's commandment, from his mother and his wife, from his sons and his daughters, from his villages and all his property, from his food and

his servants, from his friends and from everything the world possesses, he took up his cross in secret, as our Lord commanded, and went out after him entirely. As soon as he had stripped off the world and all that is in it while still alive, through the warm desire of his sincere love for Christ, he went out alone into the desert, so that he too, like our Lord, might be tempted by the Slanderer; that he might meet the passions, along with sufferings, in the wilderness, like warriors in battle; that he might take up the fight against nature and its habits; and that he might struggle like a spiritual athlete against rulers and authorities and against evil spirits, within and without. He went and lived in the desert monastery of the blessed Abraham, whom we mentioned above. It was by the small gleam of one of Abraham's signs that the blessed Rabbula had first been drawn out of the darkness of paganism into the light of truth. When he had lived with him for some time in a demanding way of life, Abraham urged him to take on a small dwelling of his own and to conduct himself in it as he wished. He obeyed his urging and took charge of a monastery. His brother lived with him, along with others, and with the blessed Eusebius, the man whom the holy Rabbula later made bishop in the city of Tella, a victor of renowned name. Their life, like that of all monasteries, was modelled on the church of the apostles, in which everything they had was held in common. Many times they would go to their night's rest without provisions, rejoicing. One day the bread ran out at their monastery, as often happened. While he was thanking his Lord who had made him worthy to bear

such sufferings with exultation, at sunset grace sent them bread for their need. Astonishing and wonderful was the strength of mind of the blessed Rabbula! For he saw this grace and said: "Because God perceived my weakness, that I am not patient under afflictions, he did this in order to test me." With this thought he took that food and gave it to others that evening, and the brothers went to sleep hungry.

When he saw that people were beginning to be drawn to him, as they are to a man who has left the world and loved the wilderness, hated himself and loved God, he did not want to be hindered in their eyes from the steady course of his righteousness. So he stole away from them and moved to the inner desert, as the blessed Antony had also done. He found a small cave in the ground, and above it a trickle of water that dripped just enough for one person. His work there was this alone: unceasing prayer, the service of the psalms, and the reading of the Scriptures. For these are the right rules of all pure monasteries and of all who belong to our Lord. This was also why he had gone there: so that the thought of God might never be cut off from his soul. For the Evil One stirred up against him there all his many and varied assaults, as that blessed man himself recounted, and fought openly against him with terrifying apparitions of many shapes. He made snakes and scorpions crawl around him and over him to frighten him, and vipers and [?] to terrify him. But all of them were defeated by the power of the seal of the cross. When Satan could not prevail by his power, he would overturn the jar

of water which that small trickle dripped for him, the measure of his need. Yet the things with which Satan fought him so harshly in order to afflict him only added greatly to his great righteousness: they made him quickly grow bold in prayer, humble himself in supplication, and take refuge with all his strength in God, that he might deliver him from every evil. For by endurance within and without he stood firm against the Evil One, valiantly, and he was ready to meet every evil impulse with every good impulse and to prevail. One day, as he stood in prayer that his answer from God might not fail, suddenly a band of Arabs appeared, coming towards him. He rejoiced, thinking that the time of his crown had already arrived. But they saw a living corpse in a bare cave, despised him and left him alone. They took only his bread and his garment and went away. For this too he thanked his Lord. He marveled at this as well: that someone who was coming to bring him bread for his need, as a grace, met them and they did him no harm, so that his endurance might triumph in both trials. While he lived in this angelic way of life in body and soul, and kept his mind directed towards God, like the angels in their service in heaven, the members of his monastery found out where he was and how he was living, and came and persuaded him to come back to them. But because the desire for martyrdom burned in his heart like a hot fire, he set out, taking the blessed Eusebius with him, and the two went down to Baalbek, the city of the pagans, and entered the temple of their idols

in their divine zeal, to smash them and be made worthy of martyrdom. They did not go there hoping to come back alive. Rather, they set out to do this in the hope that the pagans would be enraged with them and kill them, and that by being killed they would bear witness. Nor did they lack the sufferings of martyrdom. Yet they were spared, because of the things God was preparing for them in the future: that they would prosper in the office of bishop. The pagans beat them mercilessly, until they thought they were dead. Then they flung them like corpses from a great height down a long flight of steps. Their limbs were battered on the steps as they were passed down from one to the next; tumbling one on top of the other, they went down, thrown and dragged over every step, until they reached the ground. They returned to their dwelling rejoicing that they had been found worthy, for God's sake, to bear in their bodies the marks of the sufferings of Christ. They endured the afflictions of death, as they had wished, but they did not die as martyrs, as they had hoped. They were martyrs by their own will, as they had longed to be; but they were not brought to their end by being killed, because they were being preserved so that through them many might be crowned.
How the blessed Rabbula became bishop in the city of Edessa.

When Mar Diogenes, bishop of Edessa, died, the bishops gathered at Antioch, together with Acacius, bishop of Aleppo, before Alexander the patriarch, to consider whom they should install as bishop in Edessa.

And the Spirit of Jesus persuaded their hearts that Rabbula was fit to be chosen for that see, because he willed it. As over David, so over this man too the Spirit spoke through the mouth of the priests: "I have found Rabbula my servant, who is fit for my service. Anoint him by your hands with the oil of my holiness. My hand will help him, and my arm will strengthen him. I will destroy before him the enemies of the truth, and I will crush those who hate him." This was indeed fulfilled as prophesied, for he subdued the heretics by his vigour. "My faithfulness and my goodness shall be with him, and in my name his horn shall be exalted." Moved by this testimony, which the Spirit of Jesus confirmed in their souls, they sent in haste, seized him from his monastery, brought him to Antioch and made him bishop. They did not let him say, as many do for form's sake and as a pretence, "I am not able to bear the weight of authority." Indeed, it did not even occur to him to make a show of using these customary phrases, with which people make much of the occasion, find excuses and decline, saying, "We are not equal to it." For he was a spiritual man, and he felt bound not to let his heart disdain the call in any way. With a free soul he judged every matter rightly, so that no one should treat the call with contempt, as though it were not from God. For he was afraid of being found to resist, and said, "Let it not be found that I am standing against God." And he comforted himself, saying: "No desire for it ever ruled my mind at all, and the thought of it never rose in my heart. I believe without doubt that this matter is wholly and truly of God.

And since he has willed that the hard yoke of authority and the precious mystery of the priesthood be laid on my weakness, may his will be done and his pleasure fulfilled. Just as I obeyed his word and my soul went out after him from the evil world, following [?] his commandments, so now too I accept his command in faith, and I enter the world by his strength, only to do his will." When Edessa heard the good news that Rabbula had been made its shepherd, the people hurried out to meet him with joy and received him in peace. As soon as he had entered and sat upon the throne of the priesthood, amid the many acclamations with which the whole people of Edessa honoured him, he first showed his outstanding diligence regarding the glorious orders of the church's service. "If the priests of Israel served in fear and reverence in the tabernacle of meeting, how much more is it fitting for us to serve as priests in fear and love in the church of God, which he purchased with his blood." By the wisdom of God that was in him he translated the New Testament from Greek into Syriac, because of its variant readings, exactly as it was. There were many silver vessels set aside for the service of the tables [?] of the clergy; he ordered them sold at once, and they were sold. He distributed their price fairly for the relief of the needy, and gently persuaded the clergy to use earthenware vessels instead. He also considered selling the gold and silver vessels used in the service of the churches and giving their price to the poor, saying:

"It is plain to those who understand that splendid service vessels of gold and silver add nothing to the honour of God. Rather, the Spirit of God rests in pure hearts, while through contempt his commandment is scorned." But he was held back from doing this by the pleas of many, because these were the offerings of their departed forefathers, which they had offered to God for the redemption of their souls. He counselled the members of his clergy as a father counsels his children, and instructed them as a head directs its limbs, and persuaded them lovingly, saying: "You know, my brothers, that because we stand above, on the glorious height of the priesthood, the whole people standing below us looks to us and is guided by us. So let us not become a stumbling stone to anyone in any matter, nor bring a blemish on our ministry, so that the service of our Lord is insulted because of us. Let us do nothing for which we are despised by our own heart or by other people, and above all not by God. But in everything let us show ourselves to be ministers of God, in all things that are worthy of God, as the apostle said. Let us be adorned with all the fitting beauty of true righteousness, and set an example of good works in our own persons, as witnesses to those who see us that our counsel is true. Therefore I ask you, by the gentleness and humility of Christ, that before all else you keep yourselves apart from the company of women. Let none of you ever be persuaded to let his brother's daughter or his sister's daughter live with him. And if possible, and if it is not too burdensome for you, not even his mother or his sister, as befits

purity. Above all, do not diminish your dignity by being served by maidservants or worldly slaves. Rather, let your freedom be honoured by brothers who share our mystery, as befits the saints. Or serve one another, each of you living with a companion, as befits Christian love. Abstain completely from meat and fowl and from the bath, except when needed for sickness or the treatment of pains. Even with ordinary foods, take care not to overfeed the body, lest its pleasure carry you away by the impulse of the passions. Love of money and desire for possessions are foreign to our way of life; let them not even be named among you. Do not let fine clothes or costly garments cheapen the dignity of your chastity. Instead of these things, be constant in fasting and prayer and in the works of the saints. Let none of you give himself over to the lawsuits of the world or the legal cases of his kinsmen, but be occupied in reading the holy Scriptures. Do not love idle tales, do not wander about the streets of the city [?], and do not amuse yourselves with greedy, profitless chatter, like those empty people. Rather, be diligent in the service of the church of God, by day and by night and at all times. In all your conduct show the proof of good works, so that everyone may be assured by seeing you that the counsel of God is truly believed in your soul." And as the prophet testified to them in his word, saying: "If you heed me

and listen to me, you will not only eat the fat of the land, but you will also inherit the good things of heaven. But if you do not heed me and you resist, here you will be despised by us in the sight of everyone, and in the judgement of Gehenna you will be condemned before the angels and in the sight of all the worlds." Those whom his love did not win over gently, fear of him brought into subjection by force. The haughty among them he struck down justly, so that they might repent; the humble among them he honoured with discernment, so that they might be comforted. Those who lived contemptuously and exalted themselves over their companions because of their wealth he greatly despised and humbled, so that they might come to their senses. Those who, whether by choice or through poverty, conducted their lives kindly and with complete propriety, he raised up, magnified and loved, and entrusted with the leadership of the church. He took care that those chosen by his hand for the grades of the priesthood should be perfect in these virtues and in still more excellent ones. For he was anxious in his mind for a long time to find, by his inquiry, trustworthy assurance about men of integrity, so that he might bring them forward to the service of Christ. To his resolute mind it was easier to give his right hand to be cut off without pity, courageously, than to stretch it out lightly upon the head of a man who had not received the testimony of truth. For he fulfilled in deed the word of the apostle, and could never be persuaded to lay hands hastily on anyone, lest he share in other people's sins. Only a man who was free from the passions of both soul and body would he bring forward, by the laying on of his hand,

to the holy mysteries of the priesthood. With a loud voice he would proclaim before the whole church the names of all those he wished to bring into the clergy, adjuring all who heard, by the word of God, that if they knew anything in them foreign to God they should declare it. Along with this he also investigated them privately by every kind of inquiry, learning even from their own families whether they were lacking in anything. For he took the utmost care in every way that men without blemish should be offered by his hand to God, like the choice sacrifice and acceptable offering of Abel, the first priest. His concern was that, as far as human nature allows, priests in their ministry should be likened to the angels of heaven. Who could recount his constant admonitions concerning the chaste life of the men? In all the years of his life that he held the priesthood, twenty-four years, he never ceased from this admonition. We are not able to record, or to sum up briefly, the great care of his admonitions day after day. He testified to them and strove with them that they should keep entirely clear of intercourse with women. He commanded and warned them not to eat meat or to bathe while in health. He counselled and persuaded them not to be choked by the commerce of the world. He forbade them to lend money at interest or usury. He urged them with his sweet words to love one another. And he counselled them that, if possible, each of them should live

with a companion. He instructed them and asked them to be occupied in fasting and constant in prayer. He urged them to show themselves in everything, by deeds and words, to be disciples of Christ, giving instructions even about their clothing and shoes and the cutting of the hair of the head, so that they should not appear shabby. He also constantly warned the whole order of consecrated women that the face of a bride of Christ should never be seen by anyone's eyes in the market without the veil of chastity; that no mark of cheapness should appear in any of her ways; and that none of them should ever go to a gathering or to a banquet without the company of many others. He wished all the daughters under each deaconess to live with her in watchfulness, holiness and chastity, "for the concord of many," he said, "can guard them all." He was bound in every way to snatch people from sin and make them partakers of righteousness. Like a diligent shepherd who tends his flocks with care, such was the concern of this spiritual shepherd for that rational flock entrusted to him by God. He was afraid to neglect his care for it even a little, lest through carelessness, if he cared only for himself, a single soul of his people should be lost and his flock be diminished. With great vigilance he kept watch at all times and prayed for it, and was distressed in his mind lest there be anything evil in it, secretly or openly. In his love he would have accepted, if it were possible, that it should

do good while he himself became as one rejected, so good was his will toward it. With great suffering he laboured continually in prayer to God on its behalf. In the rich pastures of the holy Scriptures he fed it with his spiritual sayings, and as from a sweet stream of divine teaching he gave it drink with his living words, with all diligence: guarding the healthy with his reproofs, healing the sick with his consolations, and strengthening the weak with his encouragements, so that nothing of his flock should ever stray from his side through neglect. For his soul trusted in the blessed hope kept in store as the reward of his labour, according to the testimony of God, who said to him in the person of those like him: "Good and faithful servant, you have been faithful over a little; I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your Lord." His excellent instructions to the priests of the villages and the monasteries and to the consecrated are too many to tell; we record from them and about them as far as we are able. By the goodness of God his word was always seasoned, as with salt, and it could impart goodness to those who received it in faith. His word was trustworthy to his hearers because they saw his deeds, for his works and his words benefited everyone who heard and saw them, and were accepted by all as true witnesses. His word was awe-inspiring in its humility, venerable in its gentleness, lovable even in its rebuke, and profitable in deed to those who heard it. For

out of the abundance of his heart his lips spoke, and they urged everyone toward the splendour of his deeds. He would not allow himself to digress in his speaking, but spoke only of how a person might turn to God from evil works to works of righteousness. It was not that his knowledge of these other subjects and the like was lacking, but only what is profitable and of use to people occupied him. It never occurred to him to deck out his preaching with ornaments of costly words. For he did not speak in church to display the excellence of his wisdom and win praise for himself, like others who are despised by their hearers, but to pierce the hearts of his listeners. With his sharp words he strove to turn them from evil to good, and he was constrained to see that the glory of God should not be wronged in them. As Jeremiah the prophet was clothed with a mighty voice in his preaching, so he cried like a trumpet into the ears of the people to keep away from wickedness and from the sins that breed dissoluteness. He also rebuked those who rushed eagerly to watch the brief, disgraceful hour of spectacle in the theatre and the circus. And the loathsome spectacle of wild beasts shedding human blood in the stadium he abolished entirely by his authoritative command, contending justly and saying: "Far be it that this should happen in a city of believers, that people who in their faith eat the body of God and drink his blood should watch human flesh devoured

wickedly by savage beasts in a single hour." He showed them in his words the stains of the sins by which, without perceiving it, they were ruled in their souls through pleasure. And as one who was himself wounded on their behalf through his love for them, he grieved bitterly over those who, through their disobedience, were doing evil to the ruin of their lives. He did not admonish the people feebly to turn from their evil works, as one who merely discharges his duty by a warning; rather, so that there might be fulfilled in him what God promised through the mouth of the prophet, "If you bring forth the precious from the worthless, you shall be as my mouth," he laboured with all his strength. As for those who, having vowed virginity and holiness, were struck in their bodies by the wounds of sin, he alone could have described to us in his own words the pangs of anguish that pierced his heart on their account. Which of those sound in their way of life did he hear had fallen sick through some evil work, without being sick with him in suffering for him? Which of the disciples of Christ, when news reached him that he had stumbled from his vow or faltered in his faith, did he not burn for as with fire, in his pain over him? At all times, like a skilful physician, he knew how to deal with the varied conditions of the ailments of souls. There were times when the bitterness of mercy was needed to overthrow

wickedness: then, as with a sharp knife, he cut open the abscess of the inflammation, so that it might feel and recover. There were times when, with the rebukes of his words, which could put an end to folly, he healed the swelling of the ailment as with strong roots, so that it might repent and be helped. And there were also times when, by the gentle persuasion of his sweet sayings suited to the temperament of the foolish man, he healed the sickness of suffering as with soothing drugs, so that it might find relief and be built up. His concern in every way was this alone: that through the care of his teaching they might come to the health of repentance, of the soul that turns toward life. In these ways and in many more he constantly showed his care for his flock. For he truly feared the just sentence decreed in God's rebuke against those shepherds who neglect their flock and care only for themselves. And as one who truly believed in the just reckoning that will take place at the end with the shepherds, according to the word of our Lord testifying to them, "To whom much has been entrusted, from his hand much will also be required," so his heart was eager with all his strength, whether in word or in deed, in season and out of season, to admonish, teach and rebuke everyone with all authority, though the strength of his nature was not equal to the goodness of his will. For his good will was stronger than the strength of his nature. The consciences of the upright bear witness to this.

The outstanding deeds of Mar Rabbula the bishop himself consisted in these constant practices. He laboured at all times, exceptionally, in much fasting, while his very endurance was itself a perfect fast. Not only did he give no room in himself to indulgence by eating various foods, but even at mealtimes he could never be persuaded to satisfy his hunger. With three ounces of bread and one ordinary dish he would barely break his fast, abstaining from oil and wine. From the day the name of Christ was invoked upon him, he would not allow himself to satisfy his hunger with anything. He waged constant war against all desires by his abstinence, and he never deigned to crave even a little some contemptible pleasure and taste it. At all times he rose high and excelled greatly in his victory over these enfeebling passions, which bring the mighty low under the hard subjection of their needs. By his own example and by the scantiness of his food he taught everyone a fast that subdues the body while being free from boasting. The large gifts of various foods that many offered him in faith for his own use he would send, when he could be persuaded to accept them, to the sick and the afflicted in the hospital, and to those labouring in hardships in the scattered dwellings of the solitaries.

The entire furnishing of his humble table was this: a glass dish and an earthenware jar, with a wooden ladle. With these he also trained the members of his household, according to their strength; and they too, of their own will, were eager to embody in themselves the likeness of his excellence. In constant vigils of psalms and prayers they spent the greater part of the night with him, while all day long they laboured in the works of the cross and in reading before him. They fasted with him every day, and their food consisted of two things only, pulses and vegetables. The pallor of his face came to mark the faces of those with him as well, so that he could judge by looking at them whether they kept their strict practices. As if they were nourished from a single table, so their faces bore the same pallor. For he was eager to bind them, even in his episcopate, to the hard labours of his monastic life. The partnership that helps all good things had been given to him: the gift of the Spirit of the priesthood. This too is a wonder: that of the people who lived with him for twenty-four years, not one could become so accustomed to him over that long span of time as to come in to him freely out of familiarity, or to speak with him casually. Rather, every day their fear of him grew greater, and like those just beginning to come before him, so

their minds trembled in awe of him. Yet they were not terrified of him as of someone harsh and fearsome; they were abashed before him as before someone wise and venerable. Not only did his dignity never lie exposed to any contempt before their eyes, but he never in any way gave them cause to think ill of him even in their conscience [?]. For since he was aware of nothing hateful even within himself, how much more did he shine and stand honoured before their faces and everyone's, feared and loved at once. These members of his household, together with all his clergy, were bound by him faithfully, by the word of God, never to accept anything from anyone by way of bribe or gift. He also constantly restrained all the priests of his jurisdiction, so that none of his own people or of all his clergy dared to accept anything at all. "If they bring a gift in the name of a blessing, it is we who are honoured by them, and we ought to give. If it is an honour offered for show, it is we who hold authority, and it is fitting for us to give honour. If it is a gift given under compulsion, we who are their helpers ought to keep clear of it. In every respect, then, we are obliged to give and not to take." Which of the monks could match the great measure of his poverty? He lived as a mourner in his mind, and his constant clothing was a tunic of hair and a modest cloak. For the time of the church's service he wore in winter a single burnous he had acquired, and in summer a single paenula. The bedding

of his humble bed was only this: a bedspread of hair, a coverlet, and a small pillow cut from goat-hair cloth, scarcely enough to go under his head. For setting himself apart to pray before God, the appointed hours of the service were not enough for him. So from time to time he would set aside a week for constant prayer, confining himself in the seclusion of his dwelling away from human company, and hiding himself even from the sight of those who shared his cell. He also refrained from reading, so that, withdrawn from the voices and noise of people, in the gentle stillness of his thoughts his mind might be gathered wholly to itself, his thought awakened in the remembrance of his Lord, and his understanding kindled by the Spirit of his God, and so that his prayer might be sweet to him in his solitude; so that, like an acceptable sacrifice of pure petition, he might offer it to his Lord in the temple of his hiddenness, bearing on the hands of his mind the remembrance of the sins of the world, to receive from him the forgiveness of their sins in mercies beyond measure. In this hidden quiet of his short days of prayer, who knows how to recount the wondrous changes that the Spirit of God worked anew in his mind? Only the perfect like him, who have been schooled in the hidden mysteries of prayer; for them it is easy to discern from the savour of his words [?]. Hidden signs from the goodness of God were fulfilled in his heart. And like one whom those who eat of divine love hunger for again, and those who drink of it thirst for again, he was all the more constrained by the good desire of love for

his Lord to leave the city and the pressures of its affairs for forty days each year, and to flee eagerly far away and dwell in his monastery in the desert of Qenneshrin, where he could give himself to supplication in prayer and cry out mightily so that his petitions might be answered. Whenever he stood at the head of the people before God in prayer, from the very moment he first stood up his eyes never ceased from stifled weeping. So abundant was the flow of his tears that even the harsh and the merciless were moved at the sight of it, seeing how in the fervour of his spirit they streamed from his eyes onto his breast as he sat on the throne during the service. For with the fear and reverence that our human nature owes, and with the boldness of true love that God desires, he served as priest before him in a remarkable way. Through these heavenly practices, which were seen in this angel in the flesh, many and various kinds of healing were bestowed on the sick by the power of his prayer, and his faith drove from people the harsh afflictions caused by evil spirits. His word also proved to all who knew him, by experience, that when he was justly angry with anyone or made a firm decision, God turned with him. Therefore, out of awe, the mere name of his prayer could dissolve a quarrel between a man and his neighbour into peace. How many times the people, in the fervour of their faith in him, tore his garments out of longing, and passed the pieces among themselves, from one to another, as a grace,

so that a blessing from his garments was carried to many of them. Many people of the city and of his whole jurisdiction, in faith, even named their sons and daughters with the honoured name of Rabbula as a blessing. His flock was persuaded to take shelter under the wings of his name and his prayers, and prayed that his health might be complete and that he might be granted long life. For he was a strong wall that surrounded his whole diocese steadfastly, and it was never overcome by any of the pretexts of the enemy's cunning. Those who lived within the circuit of his boundary lived in an orderly way, in gentle tranquillity, trusting in him. With authority he restrained everyone from plunder, oppression and merciless exaction. For who would dare to rob the poor, defraud the needy or oppress his neighbour, without the justice of God being revealed upon him to his sorrow through Rabbula's zeal? The rich man who would deal wickedly with the poor was terrified and rebuked by the mere memory of him; and the man who would cheat someone lower than himself in an account shrank back and was afraid out of fear of his name. Everyone settled his dealings with his neighbour beforehand with an honest reckoning, so as not to be despised before him in judgement. The greedy mouth of oppressive men was bound by the bridle of his justice, so that their wrongful oppression of the poor could not be carried out openly. And the grasping hands of plunderers were tied by the sinews of his uprightness,

so that they could not curtail by force the livelihood of the weak. Which of the great men of his city, or of those who were accustomed to take refuge in the honoured houses of those in power, lifted up his head and muttered boastfully, and was not at once crushed by the heel of his truth, so that he repented of what he had dared? Or which of the judges [?] who held office in his days thought [?] ... about her word, and not lightly [?] ... God brought him to ... [?] to feel what he had foolishly done? Or who ... [?] all those in authority ... [?] exalted himself over his humility ... [?] and not swiftly ... [?] the justice of God, so that he repented of his sin? All the orphans and widows in his diocese lived as in a calm harbour in their hope in him, so that, sheltered in him, they were not violently harmed by the battering waves of cruel plunderers. In his days, men in the service of the army were not only restrained by fear of him from cheating craftsmen or exploiting the villagers; they were also forcibly constrained by his zeal to honour the Christian habit in anyone who wore it, however contemptible he might seem to the eye. For God had laid fear and love of him upon everyone in his order, so that many, out of shame and modesty, held back from a multitude of sins because of him. It was hard [?] for anyone to be found in his diocese ... [?] world, who would contemptuously confound the order of marriage

... [?] one, two sisters ... [?] was, having children ... [?] the first, who had died, not ... [?]. He never permitted anyone at all to take as wife his brother's daughter or his sister's daughter. Still less could it ever happen, while he was aware of it, that anyone should put away his wife on any pretext. For he did not allow anything that came to his hearing to be done contrary to the will of God. Many times, too, the mere memory of his awe-inspiring, divine zeal was enough to forestall and rebuke the hateful boldness of evils to come, so that many were never committed. For which of the foolish would be so shameless in his days as to lift up his eyes lewdly in public and gaze at the fair face of a chaste woman? When he merely remembered him, the holiness of this saint came to mind; it made the earth beneath him and the heaven above him tremble, and in calm quiet his body grew ashamed within him and fell silent. Or which of the disciples of Christ would wear fine, flowing garments, in which to appear grandly and boastfully in the streets of the city, without being ashamed of himself and scorning his desire, when he saw Rabbula's dignity and the humble habit in which he stood at the head of the people? Or which of the gluttons enslaved to the evil lordship of the belly's craving would remember the table of this radiant man, who never once satisfied his hunger, and still dare to eat greedily or drink dissolutely? For to people the fear of him

was set right, while others were kept safe by his graciousness. And which of the lovers of money, who were destroying their lives through the greed of their trade, would not have been properly taught by this nursling of God? From where did those seven thousand [?] a year come, which goodness supplied to the poor through his hand, besides the needs of the members of his household and of all the [?] of his city? Who would not at once have judged himself, condemned himself and hated his own fault, and hastened to share in the gifts of almsgiving after the example of this righteous man, who resembled God's compassion in everything? In all the years of his life he could not be persuaded to build anything on earth, except only half of the western foundation of the church building of his city, because it had been overcome by the damage that was in it [?]; and he repaired it in a few days. "We," he said, "live from what belongs to the poor, as by strict justice; they are not supported from what is ours, as though by God's justice. For it is to support orphans, widows and the needy that the church has inherited whatever faithful people have acquired. As for us administrators, the measure of our need, what the body allows us to use, we should take from it modestly, by strict justice, as no more than a share of the poor, and not according to the will of our body, which longs for what harms our spirit." As for the keenness of his knowledge and the brightness of his understanding, it would be a great matter to tell how he could grasp each person's affairs from his words, because he was filled with the Spirit of God,

and the words of liars, which boldly steal the truth, could not lead him astray with falsehoods. For through the Spirit of God's wisdom that was in him, he quickly came to know those who were judged before him, so that, their secret being bound up by their fear, they would speak the truth with their own mouths even against their will. And he no longer needed a witness to convict the accused. It was enough for him to discern by his own examination who was guilty and who was innocent, so that no judgment went out from him crookedly, but only justly. For like one who could feel men's thoughts in his mind, so by his inquiry he got to the bottom of their hidden things to learn the truth. Wisdom, understanding and great largeness of heart were given him by God, as to Solomon. There was no limit to the measure of his justice, how authoritatively it was set in force against the scornful, who in their arrogance did violence to the weak; just as there was no measure to the wealth of his kindness, how richly it overflowed upon those poor in body and in spirit who through their endurance had triumphed in the furnace of poverty. In his justice and his compassion he was guided in everything by God's will alone. He was indeed another Moses in his generation and his time, whose just zeal was hateful and odious to the wrongdoer, and whose discerning humility was despised and scorned by the arrogant. Yet

it was not only in these things that he resembled Moses, but in everything. In his struggles against the multitude of idols he resembled Joshua son of Nun, and above all he resembled the zeal of Josiah. For to him too it was said by his Lord, as to Joshua: "Be strong and of good courage and do not fear, for I am with you to help you." Just as Joshua son of Nun and Josiah found the land of Canaan defiled with every forest of paganism, so he too found the whole land of Edessa thickly overgrown with every forest of sin. For in Edessa above all the evil teaching of Bardaisan was flourishing, until it was condemned by him and he prevailed. That accursed Bardaisan had earlier, by his craft and the sweetness of his hymns, drawn to himself all the nobles of the city, behind whom he hoped to shelter as behind strong walls. For the fool supposed, as he erred and led his people astray, that by the borrowed strength of supporters he could firmly establish his error. But this wise farmer of the soil of the heart was not content merely to root out the choking tares from his land and sow good wheat, for that would have been easy; he strove by his wisdom to turn the tares themselves into wheat. That was the hard thing. So, instead of the terrifying sound of the trumpets of Joshua and his people, who shouted at the walls of Jericho so that they fell, and who destroyed the people and devoted their possessions to the Lord, this great and victorious general of Jesus Christ, with a calm

and loving voice, by the power of his God, was able quietly to tear down their meeting-house and carry all its treasure into his own church, even taking its stones for use. But for the people who belonged to it he took every care. He persuaded them gently, subdued them peaceably, and turned them to the genuine truth of the church of the apostles, as they renounced and anathematized their error. Then he baptized them into Christ and made them partakers of his ministry. In this way, through his teaching, he cleared away the multitude of idols and subjected them to the truth. Throughout all the years of his episcopate he baptized thousands of Jews and tens of thousands of heretics into Christ. Clad in that same armour of the Spirit, he was able to bring even the Arians into subjection to the truth of the exalted Trinity. He uprooted their house of prayer, drew them to himself, and joined them with the people in his flock, so that together we give equal glory to the one nature in three hypostases of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. As for the followers of Marcion, I could not show even in many words how great his care for them was. This putrid, creeping ulcer of the Marcionites' error was healed through the patient treatment of this great physician, victorious in every cure, with the help of his God and through his long-suffering toward them. For God made the fear of the holy Rabbula dwell in them, and they received his truth faithfully, renouncing their error. So too, by his divine wisdom, he brought even the insane Manichaeans to the settled mind of clear knowledge. They therefore confessed

as he wished, believed in the truth, were baptized into Christ and were added to his people. As for the shameful error and the unclean ways of the Borborians, wherever he found them he would consign them, with great compassion, to monasteries for the rest of their lives. For their madness is great, and their teaching is loathsome, foul for pure lips to speak or clean ears to hear. That is why he was zealous against them, so that they should not be found in his region at all. With regard to the Audians and the Sadducees [?] among the heretics, who had separated themselves from the communion of the church as people cut off from the truth, and had produced for themselves a false priesthood in imitation of the true one, following fabricated revelations and straying from the truth: toward people like these this true shepherd, who bore the burden of his flock, acted thus. He scattered their assembly, made them strangers to the temple they had adorned, drove them out of it, and settled in their place brothers who shared our mystery; and those of them who repented he received into his flock. In the same way he also showed his care for the Messalian heretics: he drew them to himself and persuaded them in Christ, and they accepted it gladly, renouncing their error. This true shepherd also strove to imitate the compassion of the Father in heaven, in keeping with his perfect love for God, and showed his care in deeds equally to the good and to the wicked. Therefore he did not neglect even the hard-hearted people of the children of Israel, but always bore an extra burden

for them, which could be seen in his dealings. For not only did he not deprive them of a share in the alms of his goodness, but many of them were also persuaded each year to receive joyfully the life-giving seal of Christ's baptism, through his constant admonition of them. After the blessed Rabbula had broken the arrows and bows of the enemies of truth with the shield of his faith, and had conquered the adversary of truth by the armour of God which he held, and had blown away all the chaff of error with the breath of his truth, and had cauterized the foul wounds of the blasphemers' blasphemies with the medicine of his teaching, and had made his whole flock one sound body of a perfect man, and was about to rest a little and take his ease on the gains he had won in his battles against the erring teachings, he pressed only for care for himself and for the household of faith in the things that are most perfect, warning, admonishing and urging that we must trade for heavenly gains through works of righteousness while we are in the world, so that these may be found for us at the end as a good and true guide, by which we may eagerly reach the kingdom of God. While he was thus admonishing and correcting in these things, and leading many others to the like by deeds and words, there was a certain bitter root, the one whose youthful branches, as those who truly knew him say, were devoured by the fire of lust, until he grew old and aged and was destroyed by death, and his pampered body lay down and became dung in the earth. From this man, then,

the spirit of falsehood made a cursed shoot sprout: Nestorius, the evil disciple of this Theodore. And it put into his mouth deadly fruits poisoned with hidden death. He had risen up and received the cursed seed from that man's teaching and from his conversation with him; but because he shrank from fear of men, it lay smothered and hidden in the evil soil of his heart. But when, on a certain occasion, he seized for himself the exalted throne of the high priesthood in the great royal city, the fool supposed, erring in his arrogance, that by the harsh force of authority and the aid of the nobles of the empire he could easily turn everyone to his blasphemy. From then on he dared to speak wrongly of Mary and to do injury to her offspring. I tremble even to recall his blasphemies: that he dared to say, "The blessed Mary is not the bearer of God, but bore a man. For if Mary bore the Son, then Elizabeth too bore the Holy Spirit." Nor did he tremble, in the contempt of his bitter heart, or feel shame before the word of the apostle, who said, "God sent his Son, and he came from a woman and was under the law." Instead he presumed [?] to grant the Son only an indwelling in Jesus, as the Spirit dwelt in John. And again he said that the servant who was born of the woman suffered according to his own nature the things that befell him, while the Son, he said, who dwelt in him, performed the signs he wished. But so as not to prolong the account of that accursed man's error, these things are enough to make known

to the discerning the magnitude of his wickedness. For he raved so wildly in his lifetime that he dared to set forth, by the distinction he drew in his words, two different sons, one by nature and one by grace. When these blasphemies which the rebel was uttering came to the hearing of this holy man, his heart groaned in fear and trembled. For through the wisdom of God within him he had already perceived what hateful harm was swiftly entering the flock of Christ through that shameful occasion. From then on he set himself to speak against that man's error, demonstrating his words, as by deeds, from the true testimony of the divine Scriptures: that the holy Mary is truly the bearer of God. For behold, the prophet Isaiah cries out: "A virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel," which means "God with us." And behold, Jeremiah proclaims: "Our God appeared on earth and lived among men." And behold, the apostle Paul sets his seal on the words of the prophets, making known his Lord's birth, which took place in the flesh from the seed of the house of David, and that he was made known to be the Son of God. And behold, John explains in his Gospel: "The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father." For he had said, "In the beginning was the Word," and "the Word became flesh," without his impassible nature being changed; rather, the Lord of all took the form of a servant by becoming a perfect man, without losing what he is, God, but with the singleness of his divinity and his humanity preserved. And one is the nature

and the hypostasis of the Son, enduring as he was even before he became incarnate. In this way he even suffered in the flesh by his own will, he who by nature cannot suffer. Therefore he died in the body and lived in the spirit, and preached the good news to the souls held in Sheol; and then he rose in the glory of his Father and ascended to heaven, where he always was and is for ever. These spiritual arrows, then, our blessed father drew and shot from the bow of his faith by the sharp string of his truthful tongue. In the ears of the people they passed without pain and built them up, but they struck at the heart of the one who stood in opposition, so that he might feel them and repent. At that very time a fine occasion called on him to go up there as well, and he openly rebuked the old error of the new Jew, while that rejected silver was still adorned with the priesthood. While he was still puffed up with the vanity of pride and sitting on the high throne of authority, face to face, before the eyes of the whole church assembled, with a loud voice and without fear, he firmly proclaimed the word of truth, straightening the crookedness of that man's false teaching by the true confession of his own faith. For the persuasion of many and the benefit of all, we intend also to write out, after our discourse about him, the homily which the blessed man delivered in the hearing of the tyrant in the great church of Constantinople, so that it may be plainly seen and believed by all what great boldness his word possessed with authority, from the strong testimony of his pure

conscience. Nor did he neglect to expose that man's error and make his own truth known also to the faithful, Christ-loving emperors, and to all the emperor's nobles who held authority. They received him like an angel of God and like the last of the apostles, with fear and love and with great honour; and out of the fervour of their love for him they ventured, affectionately and in faith, to kiss his hands, so that they might be blessed by him and profit. For that good man, so fair in his excellence in God, used to entice them to good works even from afar, so that often they, and many of those who served in the exalted empire of Rome, sent him many thousands in gold for the support of the poor. How much more, then, did the close fellowship of seeing him, full of benefits, and his delightful conversation with them, spur them on to every good thing through his admonition! Yet this man, who gladly accepted gold sent to him from afar, when those emperors and dignitaries in person offered him much gold, together with jewels and garments, and begged him to accept their offering, refused, saying: "Now that the matters for which they brought me up here have been made plain, I do not want them to think that I sought some borrowed guise in which I appeared to them, and that I take gifts from them." By this, because he was not belittled in anything by any one of them, and his freedom was not impoverished in the least, he was honoured and trusted all the more in their eyes. With these things, then, which we have related above,

he rebuked Nestorius and exposed his error; he bore witness against him before the people and showed forth his own true faith; he persuaded the emperors and enlightened them in his truth; he edified the nobles and confirmed them in his teaching; and he helped abundantly, in words and deeds, all who saw him in the cities he passed through as he went up and came back down, until by God's mercies he reached his own city. He persevered, while still faithfully contending with that dissolute wicked man, until the Good Shepherd who suffered for his flock rose up against him in right judgment, through the faithful and holy bishops of the south and the west, who by the guidance of the Holy Spirit cut him off and cast him out from the rank of the priesthood, while the just judgment of God is kept for him, in which he will receive sentence together with those who agree with him. But since it is impossible to describe in a long narrative our father's battle against this error, or again to examine in a few words the blessed man's struggle for the true faith of the church, the forty-six letters which he wrote to priests, emperors, nobles and monks are sufficient. If grace helps us, we are laboring to translate these from Greek into Syriac, so that they may show those who come upon them how his divine zeal burned and blazed as with fire. For in his hope and his love he was a son of Paul's faith. Though he did not pray, like the apostle, to be accursed from Christ for the sake of his brothers and kinsmen according to the flesh, yet to be sacrificed for Jesus' sake for his brothers and kinsmen

in the spirit he would many times have been eager, had it been possible. And since the times did not allow this to happen openly, he displayed it in himself through suffering embraced by choice and hardships freely accepted: through the sufferings of a continual cross he brought the days of his life out of this world. Nor was it only in these things that he resembled Paul. He also took pains to carry out the great charge that had been entrusted to him by the apostles before him, to care for the poor. Just as he, together with Paul, had received from the apostles this commandment to care for the poor, so he kept it diligently. Who could recount the great care he had for the support of the poor, and above all the exalted love he had for the holy poor? For in each of the solitary communities, the monasteries of chaste men who lived properly in seclusion, men whose bones even after their death were a sweet fragrance in Christ, a separate cell was prepared for him at his own command, as he wished. Whenever he went to visit them, to be helped in his faith by those who had fallen asleep in peace, and above all to help their sons with his admonition, he would lodge in it alone in quiet, so that he might train himself in prayer acceptable to God and find delight in his prayer. While his offerings of almsgiving were many and abundant toward everyone at all times, he longed also to pour out, in a special way, the sacrifice of his own self to Christ on behalf of all. And as the longing

of his good will toward God and toward all people prompted, he provided for the poor, his fellows, from his Lord's goods for as long as he lived in the world, according to God's will. And after his death he left them a good inheritance of prayer and entrusted them to the goodness of God, the mother of all, from which they might be supplied every day with what they need. For because the fire of his love lives and is kept alive in their hearts, the cherished remembrance of the beloved name of Rabbula has also nourished and kindled the fire of love for him in their hearts. That is why all the needy trade on it as on a good, full measure: the good name supplies the need of their distress. For as soon as his friends hear the delightful name of Rabbula, love for him blazes up in their hearts, their compassion grows warm, and they give alms; the receiver rejoices, the giver is helped, and God is glorified. And as the labour of our father Rabbula is kept, so on this account too it is kept before his Lord, as it is said of the faithful: "Blessed is the servant for whose sake his Lord's name is glorified." Out of the love for the poor that he had in his soul, he made an excellent change in the hospital of his city, which until then had existed only in name and not in fact. He made it truly worthy of the glory of God and fittingly to his own credit. He set apart for it certain villages from the estates of his church, so that the cost of its expenses could be met from their revenues; and a door was opened for many to bequeath to it properties and possessions, so that the sum of its revenues came to a thousand dinars a

year. From these, through his provision, the sick found rest and the healthy found help. For which of those of ill will who were not convinced would not have been persuaded by the various foods that were given to the sick through the care his command provided? For no one could have told from its pleasantness that the sick and the afflicted lay there in groups, because of the care and cleanliness they received by his command. Their beds were pleasant with soft coverings spread over them, and no filthy or worn-out garments were to be seen on them or among them at all. For the comfort of their care and the needs of their afflictions, faithful attendants and true stewards were put in charge of them by him, together with modest brothers full of love, so that they would do nothing else but serve them. He did the same in the women's hospital, which had not existed at all, but was quickly built at his command from the stones of four idol temples which were destroyed in his city by his authoritative word. In it he also appointed, specially, upright deaconesses together with women of the covenant, so that they might modestly and readily fulfil the service of caring for them. Moreover, out of God's love for those who shared his nature, kindled and blazing in him compassionately as with fire, he showed his great care above all for the poor afflicted with leprosy, who lived apart outside the city as people hated and despised.

He put a true deacon in charge of them, living beside them with upright brothers who were appointed to serve them. All the needs of their want were faithfully supplied from the church within the city, while he himself refreshed their souls at all times by deed and word. By the deed of his gift he relieved the suffering of their pains, and by the word of God he encouraged their minds, so that they would not be choked by sickness. And often, as a consolation to their souls, he gave the peace of the holy kiss upon the decaying lips of men whose bodies were rotting away. So that they would not lose heart under God's chastening of them, he strengthened them; and so that they would thank our Lord all the more for their afflictions, he urged them, saying: "Remember, my brothers, that it is written that Lazarus, because he endured evils, was counted worthy to rest in Abraham's bosom in the place of the kingdom." In all these things, then, and in many others like those we have mentioned, and in the rest which we are not able to recount, the true priesthood of that radiant man triumphed in its renown: the wicked and the insolent trembled at his justice, and the weak and the poor were supported by his gifts; he graciously inclined his ear to the oppressed, and the vindication of the wronged rested on his zeal; he encouraged the good, being an example to them in word and deed, and always gave the humble a hand to raise them up; he embodied the works of the law in his own person

and wrapped himself in his Lord's commandment like a garment; the likenesses of the friends of his God were seen in him, and he overflowed abundantly upon the districts of his diocese; all the families of the land of Edessa gloried and took pride in him, while he gloried in his Lord and was strengthened; he saw God's saving deeds with an unveiled eye, and never trusted in any righteousness of his own. After all these things, it happened, as was usual with him, that he fell ill in body, on the first day of the month of Tammuz, at the completion of twenty-four years and three months of his life in the episcopate. This too deserves to be considered and admired: the wondrous sign that occurred with him. A man who all his days had suffered from various illnesses, on the day this last illness came upon him, immediately had it revealed to him, and he said in the presence of his relatives: "The time of my rest has come upon me." He showed it in deeds as well, like one who truly sensed in his spirit that the seal of his life was approaching: the alms he was accustomed to distribute every year in the months of Kanun, he hastened to provide quickly in the month of Tammuz. He sent his alms at once by his deacons, giving to the north and the east as was his custom; and he sent others, carrying his kindness, to the monasteries in the west and the south, whose dwellers rely on the hope of God's goodness, even to the holy poor who live in the desert of Jerusalem, for whom, as it is written, the blessed Paul too collected gifts. Others went out

to the territory of all the cities under his authority. Others distributed to the priests and to the members of the covenant, men and women, in his jurisdiction. He gave to the mourners and monks in his region, and supported the poor in the villages throughout the land of Edessa. Others again distributed in his city to all the needy, to the monks, and to the covenant of men and women. He also provided for the widows and the afflicted as he wished, and he enrolled many more in addition to them. He forgave all the debts he had inherited and tore up the bonds of loans of much gold owed by craftsmen. And with his own hand he gave a blessing to all the clergy alike. When he had fulfilled all his good will and completed all his noble desire, and saw that he had rebelled against the world and its cares, despised the Evil One and his enticements, and scorned the body and its passions, he raised his voice confidently, from the good testimony of his excellent works, glorying in the Lord, as the victorious Paul said: "I have fought the good fight, I have finished my race, I have kept my faith; and from now on there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which my Lord will give me on that day, he who is the just judge. And into his hand I commit my spirit." He said these things as he prayed in the hour of his death; then he sealed his face with the cross, lovingly blessed those standing before him, and joyfully gave up his soul to his Lord. When, on the seventh day of the month of Ab, he flew off from his city into the good repose of his death, immediately its walls shook and its inhabitants trembled at the sound of the groaning lament

of its people, for in the agony of their wailing each person's voice was bound to his neighbour's and went on without ceasing. The whole city became one great mourning, divided into eighteen choirs of deaconesses within the courts of the church, while the Jews mourned outside. The whole city wept for him in the streets, in the courtyards and inside the church, with choking laments that produced bitter groans and painful tears: priests with all the people of the covenant, and laypeople together with Jews. They cried woe upon themselves, saying: "Our loss has struck all of us! What a lover of God and lover of mankind we have been robbed of! What a true shepherd and head of righteousness has left us orphans! What a provider of good things, who bore the burden of the community, has been taken from us! What a scribe of truths, firm in his faith, has been parted from us! What a counsellor of fair things and encourager of excellent things has been emptied out of our midst! Who will follow after him in his works for us," they said, "this physician of mercy, who held the sufferings of those who shared his nature in his heart? For he was a father to orphans in his love for them, a brother to the poor in his care for them, a companion to mourners in his humble ways, and a lover of the holy in his excellent discernment; and in his truth he felt bound to care for the life of everyone." These things they said as they wept for themselves, and they repeated words like these as their souls ached. On the following day they hastened to lay his pure body in a wooden coffin

from within his own monastery, so that his holy body would not be torn apart by the hands of all the people, who were pressing in their love to take a blessing from him in faith. And so they escorted him with psalms and hymns, processing in splendour, to the haven of the tomb in our cemetery, into which the toil-laden ship of his blessed old age came down, carrying within it a great cargo of righteousness. From it help is distributed to those who in faith ask his Lord in his name to grant them, through his true treasurer, the gift of mercies from the treasury of his grace. For behold, the sick come there and are healed; the healthy come there and are helped; demons too are there and are driven out; the oppressed are there and are comforted; the poor are there and are supported; and the rich as well, and they are enriched. For he is a spring of blessings, even his cold remains, because of the fervour of the Spirit by which he was refreshed. And by his Lord's permission he has been given authority over the fullness of his treasures, from which he may abundantly supply good things to all who come to him as needy. For he has gathered his own wealth fully to himself, and the whole labour of his races is kept perfectly with him, until his body is raised and renewed, and his soul is made new in it and shines, so that, complete with them, he may delight in glory on the day of the glorious revelation of the Son of God, the Saviour of all. May he, by the gift of his mercies, make us all worthy by his grace to stand at his right hand under the peaceful protection of our victorious father, and may our father say on our behalf to his Lord, with unveiled face, [?] in us:
"Behold, I, my Lord, and the children whom you have given me." You we worship, to your Father we give thanks, and your Holy Spirit we glorify, now and for ever and ever. Amen.
Here ends the account of the triumphs of Mar Rabbula.
The bishop.
